sources.fact: Scientific American, 'Do Women Who Live Together Menstruate Together?': menstrual synchrony was first demonstrated in a 1971 paper in Nature by Martha McClintock, who asked 135 college girls living in dorms; a later study following 186 female students in dorms for a year saw no evidence, but plenty of random overlaps; women often have cycles of different lengths, so they randomly phase in and out of synchrony

Live Science, 'Women's Periods Don't Really Sync Up When They Live Together' (2017): Clue app and University of Oxford study of 360 pairs of women; 273 pairs' cycles diverged, just 79 converged; living together did not increase the likelihood of cycle alignment; overlapping menses are not surprising because two cycles are on average about a week apart and a period typically lasts at least five days
FIGO, 'Period syncing myth debunked': out of 1,500 responses there were 360 pairs; 273 pairs had larger gaps between start dates, just 79 got closer together

post.instagram_caption:
Do periods really sync when you live together? 📅

The idea comes from a 1971 study of 135 college students in dorms. Later studies didn't find it: an app study with University of Oxford researchers tracked 360 pairs of women, and about 76% drifted further apart. Living together didn't make syncing more likely.

Cycles have different lengths and periods last several days, so overlaps happen by pure chance.

Sources: Scientific American, Live Science, FIGO.

Did you ever think your period synced with someone's?
